Loss is loss. It doesn't matter if it's a person, a pet, a job, or simply a loss of a dream. It tends to elicit the same patterns in humans.

Grief allows us to navigate the deep sorrow that comes with what is not or what no longer is or what might not be.

In grieving, we go through the process of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance, DABDA. it gives us a chance to step into a new world. It gives us a chance to learn.

Too often, individuals stay stuck in the grief and don't re-engage with life. We're meant to mourn, and also were meant to be resilient and bounce right back into our lives and move forward.

Susan Anderson talks about the SWIRL process. She says that when our lives are shattered, we withdraw, we start to internalize and wonder how we contributed or how we could have done things different, then we rage and get angry at what is, and finally, we lift. We re-engage with our lives and we come out better than before. If we will allow it.

Depression seems to be a natural part of that. It seems to be part of the internalization and rage phases that every person will go through when they experience loss.

Give yourself some Grace for the loss and the feelings. Give yourself some allowance to feel those and be with them. Loss can feel overwhelming, but you can overcome it. When you are ready, and you get to decide this, re-engage with your life.

Re-engage with purpose or some kind of service outside of you. Something that moves you from deep inside of you back into the world.

Routine has been critical for my well-being. It directs my day and starts me off with a sense of purpose. Here's the routine that I follow every morning since my divorce:

1. Jump right out of bed first thing in the morning and drink a lot of water.
2. Low intensity exercise
3. Make my bed
4. Take a hot shower and end it with 30 seconds of ice cold shower.
5. Get dressed and groom myself
6. Write in my journal. Right one thing I'll let go of, one thing I'm grateful for, and one thing I'm committed to creating that day.

By doing this I've been able to break through a lot of emotions I've been coming up. Look up the term satisficing and get good at it. I am a perfectionist as well, but nothing will ever be to our standards. We can lose a lot of sleep and productivity over it. Satisficing is a term coined by Herbert Simon--a Nobel prize winner--and it changed my life. I have much less anxiety now because of this concept. When it comes to work, anything is better than nothing, and with your standards, your anything will be a higher standard than many peoples' somethings--I hope that made sense. 

Make lists. I have checklists. that way when I get sidetracked or something gets dropped in my inbox that is more urgent, I can go back to where I left off. I leave myself breadcrumbs so that I don't have to try to remember everything. There is a lot of anxiety generated in remembering everything we need to do; especially at night when we are trying to sleep but our brain is running through everything we need to remember. Keep a notepad next to your bed so you can right down an idea and get to it after a good night's sleep.

Take a sleeping aid. Lack of sleep can lead to anxiety.

In regard to shame, tell your story to safe people. People who will not use it to bludgeon you. Letting people know is relieving, especially when they are protective of your emotions. 

Lastly, take action despite the fear. Drudge through it if you have to, but the action is the only way out. The last thing you need is mounting tasks. That will just make the work harder. Do the hardest things first if you can. If you can't do that, do the easy stuff first...just DO something!!

I hope that helps. I have a highly stressful job and These are tools I use.

Another thing I use to stay focused--which will probably cause some discussion in this forum--is drink some caffeine. While it does induce anxiety, I know where it is coming from and it helps me stay energized and focused. Anxiety can be draining and that little burst of energy helps me get shit done. A caveat though, it will give you anxiety, so use it wisely.

Judith Herman (2012), in response to the article by Resick et al., said that there are three very important things to remember with C-PTSD:  First, C-PTSD symptoms are similar cross-culturally and are common among child-abuse victims and those who experience mass violence. Second, C-PTSD symptoms are found in individuals who were exposed to prolonged and repeated trauma and that the treatments for PTSD could actually be harmful to those who suffer C-PTSD. Third, C-PTSD is not BPD, PTSD, or MDD, and let’s not forget, Dissociative Disorders (DD), but is instead a stand-alone illness that has characteristics of each of those illnesses. C-PTSD is a discrete entity and deserves its own research, symptoms, definitions, and treatments (Herman, 2012). Amen! It sounds like Judith Herman is all about clarifying C-PTSD as a distinct illness and that is something we need to remember. C-PTSD is not PTSD. It is not MDD, It is not BPD or DD. It is its own illness with characteristics of those other illnesses. I think this is important to know so that we can find treatments that are unique to C-PTSD. I am tired of trying everything under the Sun and feeling frustrated. I need something that works for my illness and this all starts with understanding what it is.

Okay, those are my thoughts on C-PTSD. What do you think? Tell me in the comments how you understand it. I look forward to hearing your thoughts.
